title: Onboard sensory map and workload triage — 72hr kit
content:
Purpose: fast, low-friction immersion for new engineers/product/pm hires that reduces sensory overload and surfaces hidden blockers in the first 72 hours. This doc is a lightweight kit engineers and mentors can use to run a quiet first-3-day onboarding with explicit workload triage, a sensory map for signals to watch, and simple acceptance criteria for day 3.

Quick notes to owner:
- This is intentionally short and modular — copy the checklist into calendar invites.
- Primary audience: hiring manager + assigned mentor + new hire.
- Goals: 1) safe first commit + one small cross-team call, 2) surface infra/network/permission blockers, 3) set clear 30/60/90 expectations and a first-week focus.

Day 0 (pre-start checklist — to be completed by people-ops / IT before 1pm start):
- hardware/access: laptop imaged, VPN profile preloaded, ssh key installed (yes/no)
- accounts: GitHub org invite sent; Slack invite sent; SSO group assignment verified
- calendar: intro 30m with manager scheduled; mentor 1:1 scheduled; team standup invite added
- tangible deliverable queued: tiny repo + readme with 3-step run instructions

Day 1 (sensory map + micro-rituals):
- 09:00 - 09:20: welcome + sensory map orientation (mentor + hire)
  - Sensory map: quick inventory of the new hire's noise surface: email volume, build log frequency, alerts they see, number of Slack channels. Rate each 1-5.
  - Call out top 3 anxieties: deployment risk, infra flakiness, unclear routing for questions.
- 09:30 - 10:30: hands-on tiny repo run (must run locally + basic test pass)
- 11:00 - 11:20: infra checklist (SRE on-call quick sync if needed). Record any failed permissions.
- 14:00 - 15:00: shadow session: follow engineer on a short pairing task (no pressure to ship).
- End-of-day: write 3 signals to doc: success signal, friction signal, blocker signal.

Day 2 (workload triage & lightweight onboarding experiments):
- Morning: triage board (kanban) seeded with tasks that are safe_{visibility=low} but meaningful (docs fix, small test, add a logging statement). Priority: safety < confidence < speed.
- Mentor and hire run a 30m retro on matching expectations vs reality. Capture unknown unknowns and who will resolve them.
- Introduce the regional routing policy notes (how requests hit serving clusters) — 15m explainer tailored to role.

Day 3 (acceptance & handoff):
- Morning: quiet acceptance checklist (pass if at least 3 of 4 criteria met):
  1) completed tiny repo change merged or approved as a draft PR
  2) 1 internal cross-team message sent and context recorded
  3) any infra blockers have an assigned owner and ETA
  4) first-week OKR focus set (3 items)
- 11:00 - 11:30: manager sync to agree on 30/60/90 focus and clear next actions
- End-of-day: mentor handoff note published to the team channel with a one-paragraph summary of progress and remaining risk.

Scoring rubric (lightweight, to avoid checkbox theatre):
- Green: new hire completed repo run, merged a doc/test PR, communicated to one cross-team owner, no unresolved infra blockers.
- Yellow: progress made, at least one friction signal remains (e.g., missing access) with an owner and ETA.
- Red: major blocker unresolved (no owner / >72h ETA) or hire unable to run the tiny repo due to infra issues. Immediate escalation to IT + SRE.

Interview/hiring signal tie-ins (people-ops guidance):
- Use this kit to set realistic acceptance criteria at offer stage. In offer packet include a single line: "72hr quiet-launch target: small repo run + cross-team intro + blocked items assigned."
- For high-priority roles, add a pre-board task: ensure the tiny repo contains a structured README + one test and is accessible to contractor/offer-stage candidates for a short pre-start smoke test.

Mentor rotation protocol (practical):
- Primary mentor: daily for first 3 days, then every other day week 1–2.
- If primary mentor is overloaded, assign a shadow mentor who will take the daily micro-sync.
- At day 3, mentor must post a 3-line status message to the hiring manager and people-ops.

Workload triage playbook (how we reduce cognitive load):
- Acceptable first-week tasks: docs updates, test stabilization, tiny observability hooks, a solo smoke test. No production deploys first week unless cleared by manager + SRE.
- If number of incoming channels > 6 (Slack + 5 others), reduce alerts by triaging to a read-only digest for the new hire and assign an "alert pilot" for them (one person who filters noise).

Notes to people-ops / hiring managers:
- Common friction we see: delayed GitHub org invites, MFA complications, Docker image pulls blocked by firewall. Log each instance as JIRA-ONB-[incremental id] so we can trend.
- Run a lightweight 72h retro after each onboarding and add the top 3 action items to the on-call onboarding backlog.

Templates (copy/paste into invites):
- Sensory map template (1-5 scale): email volume __, build failures ___, number of active Slack channels ___, production alert frequency ___, number of direct reviewers ___ 
- End-of-day note template: 1) what I ran, 2) what blocked me, 3) who I need help from tomorrow.

Open questions / experiments to run:
- Can we automate account provisioning test and surface a green/red via a bot before start? (experiment Q1-2026)
- Try a "quiet intro" cohort where 3 hires start the same day with staggered mentor hours to reduce single-mentor overload. Measure day-3 acceptance rates.

Appendix: quick escalation matrix
- Infra pull/dns/certs: tag @sre-core and file JIRA-ONB-XXXX
- Access / SSO issues: people-ops -> IT ticket with priority "onboard-critical"
- Legal / laptop procurement: people-ops -> vendor ops

Last updated: small revisions to mentor rotation cadence on 2025-11-18 by Maya Chen.
